heading: Carts, travois and the ulu
intro: Métis, Niitsitapi (Blackfoot) and Inuit tools each move a load or split a material with a force, just like the machines in this lab. A Red River cart turns on a wheel and axle, a travois lets a dog or horse drag a family's belongings to a new camp, and an ulu presses a curved blade straight down. Each connection names the people whose technology it is, with a source for each claim.

connections.title: Red River carts at Fort Edmonton
connections.text: Fort Edmonton Park says the Métis built a thriving community close to Fort Edmonton. Métis buffalo hunters travelled through Edmonton with their Red River carts and stopped at the fort to sell meat, fish and pemmican. The Carlton Trail, the most important long cart road, ended at Fort Edmonton. Each cart rolls on two wooden wheels turning on a wooden axle. Lawrence Barkwell of the Louis Riel Institute writes that dish-shaped spoked wheels did not sink as far into the earth. Grease could not be used because it would pick up dust and dirt. The City of Edmonton names its Métis ward "to honour a cornerstone in Edmonton's history."

sources.title: Fort Edmonton Park: Métis in Treaty 6 and Relationship to Fort Edmonton Park (Métis community near the fort; Red River carts through Edmonton; selling meat, fish and pemmican)
The Canadian Encyclopedia: Red River Cart (Carlton Trail ended at Fort Edmonton; carts used mainly by Métis; axles not greased)
Lawrence J. Barkwell, Louis Riel Institute, Red River Cart (dish-shaped spoked wheels; no grease on axles; Fort des Prairies, now Edmonton): metismuseum.ca
Indigenous Peoples Atlas of Canada: Red River Carts (two wooden wheels, wooden axle, the main Métis inland transport)
Source of the Métis ward name ("to honour a cornerstone in Edmonton's history"): City of Edmonton, Transforming Edmonton, Métis Ward: How river lots shaped Edmonton

connections.title: Siksika travois: dogs, horses and the elk dog
connections.text: Blackfoot Crossing Historical Park, in Siksika Nation, is the site where Treaty 7 was signed. The park explains that dogs carried loads on their backs or were trained to pull a travois: two long poles whose front tips met at the dog's shoulders. A dog travois could carry a load of 60 pounds or more. The park says people who first saw horses called them po'no'komita, "elk dog," because they were the size of an elk. The Canadian Encyclopedia says horses let families move larger tipis and more belongings. Glenbow's Niitsitapiisini site says women loaded the travois and led the dogs and horses, and that loads could tip on slopes.

sources.title: Source of the word po'no'komita (elk dog) and the dog travois (two poles, 60 or more pound load): Blackfoot Crossing Historical Park, Imitaa (Dogs)
Blackfoot Crossing Historical Park: home page (in Siksika Nation; site of the signing of Treaty No. 7)
The Canadian Encyclopedia: Travois, by René R. Gadacz (dog and horse travois; Siksika platforms; horses allowed larger tipis)
Glenbow, Niitsitapiisini: Our Way of Life, How We Moved Camp (women loaded the travois; loads could tip on slopes)

connections.title: The ulu: a curved blade pressed straight down
connections.text: CBC reports that uluit are household items regularly used by Inuit across the North. The Canadian Encyclopedia says ulu means "woman's knife" in Inuktitut. An ulu has a thin, crescent-shaped blade with the handle on top. Its shape varies by community and region, and the Inuinnait (Copper Inuit) made blades from local copper. A University of Waterloo chemistry article explains that the ulu is pressed straight down, which gives "the most efficient force." Nancy Etok, interim president of Pauktuutit Inuit Women of Canada, says mass producing the ulu "will shadow the real purpose and real importance of what the ulu means to Inuit."

sources.title: CBC News: This American company is selling 'ulu-inspired knives.' Inuit say that's not right (uluit used across the North; Nancy Etok quote)
Source of the meaning of ulu (woman's knife): The Canadian Encyclopedia, Ulu (shape, regional variation, Inuinnait copper blades)
University of Waterloo, Centre for Advanced Science Education: Ulu: chemistry and Inuit women's culture (pressing straight down gives the most efficient force)
Canada's History: As Sharp As Ever, by Amelia Fay (semicircular blade; uluit still important in traditional activities)

try: A Red River cart is a wheel and axle. In the lab, a wheelbarrow's wheel mostly makes rolling easier instead of multiplying force. Is the same true for the cart? Barkwell writes that the axles turned without grease, wood rubbing on wood. Use Lesson 4: how would that friction change the input work, the output work and the efficiency? Why would wheels that do not sink as far into the earth lower the force a horse or ox needs?

A dog pulls a travois with a 60 pound load (about 27 kg). Use Lesson 1 to find the load's weight in newtons. Then use made up numbers: if the dog pulls with 90 N for 2 km to a new camp, how much work does it do? Glenbow says loads could tip on slopes. Going up a hill, which force on the travois points uphill and which points downhill?

An ulu blade is a wedge: a moving inclined plane. When you press straight down, which way does the blade push the material? Use the gallery in Lesson 3 to explain how a wedge changes the size or the direction of your force. Why might pressing straight down above the blade waste less of your force than pushing on a knife handle held off to one side?

slide.title: Carts, travois and the ulu
points: Edmonton: Métis hunters brought Red River carts, a wheel and axle, through Edmonton to Fort Edmonton.
Alberta: Siksika dogs and horses pulled travois loads; the park says horses were called po'no'komita, "elk dog."
Canada: Inuit press the curved ulu blade straight down, a wedge that splits and cuts.
slide.notes: Use with Lesson 3 (The six simple machines) to sort each tool: the Red River cart is a wheel and axle and the ulu blade is a wedge. Use the cart again with Lesson 4 (Work in, work out): its ungreased wooden axle shows friction turning some input work into heat. The travois suits Lesson 2 (Work) and Investigation 4 (Work around Alberta): students find a dog's work with W = F × d. Compare the cart's wheel with the wheelbarrow in Lesson 7 (Complex machines). Point students to the Ways of knowing section in the lab for sources and discussion prompts.

review_flags: Existing content: I found no Indigenous content in the Machines and Work Lab or the deck, sourced or unsourced. The canoe paddle (Lesson 5: "Some tools, like a canoe paddle or a snow shovel, have an MA less than 1"; also the Coverage note for F2.K5 and the deck's mechanical advantage slide notes) and loading a canoe (Investigation 4 site file and deck notes: "loading a canoe up a plank (300 N up 1.5 m: 450 J)") are generic Alberta contexts with no Indigenous attribution. I think they need nothing: they make no claim about any people, so there is nothing to source. I did not add a canoe connection because I fetched no source on canoes in this task, and attaching the canoe to a nation without one would be a guess. If you want one later, a nation or Métis source on birchbark canoes would be needed.

Science framing: I call the Red River cart a wheel and axle and the ulu blade a wedge. Those are my classifications for the lab, not claims in the sources. I did not call the travois a simple machine; the try prompt uses it for work and force only. Please confirm you are comfortable with that framing. The cart prompt deliberately mirrors the lab's wheelbarrow note (the wheel mainly reduces rolling friction).

Load numbers conflict across sources, so the Edmonton text gives none: The Canadian Encyclopedia says loads as heavy as 450 kg; the Indigenous Peoples Atlas says 300 to 450 kg, almost 500 kg with oxen; USask News says about 1,000 pounds with oxen and close to 500 pounds with a horse; Barkwell quotes Alexander Henry (1802) as five pieces of 90 pounds per horse. For the travois, The Canadian Encyclopedia says 20 to 30 kg for a dog travois and Blackfoot Crossing says 60 pounds or more. I used Blackfoot Crossing's figure (Siksika source) and turned it into about 27 kg in the try prompt. Please check the conversion wording.

Names and words: po'no'komita ("elk dog") is spelled as on the Blackfoot Crossing page; please confirm the spelling with Siksika. Glenbow gives Niitsitapi as "Real People" and niitoy-yiss as tipis; I did not use either in the text. The Canadian Encyclopedia says ulu means "woman's knife" in Inuktitut, while Canada's History says it is "sometimes referred to as a woman's knife". I used the Encyclopedia wording; you may prefer the softer one. I wrote uluit as used by CBC and Canada's History; no source I fetched states outright that it is the plural, so I did not say so. I added Inuinnait (Copper Inuit) to peoples because the Encyclopedia names them for copper blades.

Edmonton: the Carlton Trail ending at Fort Edmonton comes from The Canadian Encyclopedia; Barkwell names "Fort des Prairies (now Edmonton)". The Fort Edmonton Park page has no author or date. It also says many Métis were forced from their homes onto road allowances; I left that out of a machines lab, but it may belong in a Métis focused lesson with Métis Nation of Alberta input. The City of Edmonton quote is from its Métis ward naming page.

A University of Alberta Faculty of Native Studies Red River cart page (sites.google.com/ualberta.ca) appeared in search but needs a login, so I did not cite it. If the Faculty has a cart on campus, it would be a strong, truly local Edmonton example. Could you check?

Not used: a Global News story (2021) on carts built at Rocky Mountain House with Métis Nation local 845. The builder is not described as Métis and the headline frames it as a "lost art" (deficit framing), so I left it out. Qamutik: the only source I fetched was a museum catalog record for a model, with no Inuit voice, so I did not use it. Mari King's Pitt Rivers Museum dog travois lesson names no Blackfoot collaborators, so I did not cite it.

Sources: the ulu force claim comes from a University of Waterloo chemistry article by non Inuit authors; the Inuit voices come from CBC (Nancy Etok of Pauktuutit). Would you like to invite an Inuit Knowledge Keeper (for example through an Edmonton Inuit organization), a Métis cart builder through the Métis Nation of Alberta, or Blackfoot Crossing Historical Park's education staff to share about these tools? Glenbow's Niitsitapiisini pages do not say on the page I fetched who wrote them, though the toolkit is Blackfoot focused.

The travois text uses past tense for historical travel by dog and horse; The Canadian Encyclopedia notes some rural hunting parties still use the travois. The ulu text is in present tense because uluit are in everyday use. Please confirm the tense choices read respectfully.
